questions.stem: Which of the following best defines contingency planning?
options: Preparing in advance a response to a possible future event that would seriously disrupt the business
Responding to a crisis as it unfolds
Forecasting next year's sales as accurately as possible
Insuring all of a business's non-current assets
questions.why: Contingency planning happens before the event; the plan is prepared for something that may or may not occur.
whyNot: That is crisis management, which happens during the event.
Sales forecasting predicts the expected outcome rather than planning for disruption.
Insurance is one possible response within a plan, not the plan itself.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines risk assessment?
options: Identifying the risks a business faces and judging each by likelihood and impact
Calculating the insurance premium a business must pay
Estimating the profit a business will make next year
Recording accidents that have already happened
questions.why: Likelihood and impact are the two dimensions that turn a long list of risks into a usable plan.
whyNot: Premiums are a cost of one response to risk, not the assessment itself.
Profit forecasting is a different exercise.
Recording past events is incident reporting rather than forward assessment.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines business continuity planning?
options: Planning how essential operations will continue during and after a major disruption
Planning how to expand a business into new markets
Planning the annual budget for each department
Planning which employees will be promoted next year
questions.why: Continuity planning asks what the business must keep doing whatever happens, and how.
whyNot: That is growth strategy.
That is budgeting.
That is succession planning, which is related but narrower.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines succession planning?
options: Identifying and developing employees who can fill key roles when the current holders leave
Deciding who inherits the shares of a deceased owner
Choosing which products will replace those being withdrawn
Planning the order in which loans will be repaid
questions.why: Succession planning addresses the risk of losing key people, which the specification includes and students routinely omit.
whyNot: That is a legal and personal matter rather than a business plan.
That is product portfolio management.
That is debt management.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the correct list of the four standard responses to a risk?
options: Avoid, reduce, transfer, accept
Identify, measure, report, audit
Plan, do, check, act
Forecast, budget, monitor, review
questions.why: Each risk can be avoided, reduced, transferred through insurance or contract, or simply accepted where action would cost more than the expected loss.
whyNot: Those are stages of risk reporting rather than responses to a risk.
That is a general quality improvement cycle.
Those are budgetary control steps.

questions.stem: A risk is very unlikely but would close the business if it happened. What is the appropriate response?
options: Plan for it, because high impact justifies preparation even when likelihood is low
Ignore it, because the likelihood is low
Accept it, because unlikely risks never occur
Treat it as equivalent to a frequent minor risk
questions.why: Plan for impact as well as likelihood: a low-probability event that would end the business is worth insuring against.
whyNot: Ignoring a business-ending risk leaves the whole business exposed.
Low probability is not zero probability.
A frequent minor risk can be absorbed; a business-ending one cannot.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes risk transfer?
options: Shifting the financial consequences to another party, usually through insurance or a contract clause
Reducing the likelihood of the risk occurring
Stopping the activity that creates the risk
Deciding to bear the risk without action
questions.why: Transfer moves the financial loss elsewhere, though it does not restore lost customers or reputation.
whyNot: That is risk reduction.
That is risk avoidance.
That is risk acceptance.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a cost of contingency planning?
options: Holding spare capacity, inventory or cash that earns nothing
The loss caused by the disruptive event itself
The cost of recruiting replacement staff after a resignation
The interest charged on a long-term loan
questions.why: Contingency planning ties up resources continuously for an event that may never happen, which is why it is so often under-done.
whyNot: That is the cost of the event, which is what the plan is designed to reduce.
That is a labour turnover cost, not a planning cost.
Interest is a financing cost unrelated to contingency planning.

questions.stem: Why is the best-known benefit of contingency planning described as speed?
options: In a crisis, the business with a plan acts while the business without one holds meetings
Planning makes the disruptive event happen sooner
Planning reduces the time needed to prepare the annual accounts
Planning speeds up product development
questions.why: The decisions have already been taken, so the response begins immediately, which is where most of the loss reduction comes from.
whyNot: Planning does not affect whether or when the event occurs.
Accounts preparation is unrelated.
Product development is a separate activity.

questions.stem: Why can a contingency plan create false confidence?
options: A document nobody has rehearsed is not a capability
Plans are legally binding once written
Plans always predict the wrong event
Plans make insurance unnecessary
questions.why: Rehearsal is what turns a written plan into an actual ability to respond, which is why testing is part of continuity planning.
whyNot: Internal plans are not legally binding documents.
Plans may prove to cover the wrong event, but not always.
Insurance often remains part of the plan rather than being replaced by it.

questions.stem: Why is a founder-dominated small business particularly exposed to the loss of a key person?
options: The more decisions run through one person, the greater the risk of losing them
Small businesses are legally required to have one decision maker
Small businesses cannot buy insurance
Founders are more likely to leave than other employees
questions.why: It links to the power culture and the entrepreneur-to-leader transition: concentrated authority creates a single point of failure.
whyNot: No such requirement exists; the concentration is a choice or a consequence of size.
Insurance is available, including key person cover.
The issue is the concentration of authority, not the probability of departure.

questions.stem: A resort island depends on one generator, one water plant and one transfer operator. What does this illustrate?
options: Single points of failure, where continuity planning concentrates on duplication
Economies of scale, where larger operations reduce unit costs
Diseconomies of scale caused by poor communication
Price elasticity of demand for a luxury service
questions.why: Any one failure stops the whole operation with guests already on site, so the plan is to duplicate each critical element.
whyNot: Scale economies concern unit costs, not resilience.
Diseconomies concern the problems of large size.
Elasticity concerns demand response to price.

questions.stem: What is the cleanest way to frame the core trade-off in contingency planning?
options: A certain small cost now against an uncertain large cost later
A certain large cost now against a certain small cost later
An uncertain small benefit now against a certain large benefit later
A fixed cost now against a variable cost later
questions.why: That framing comes from risk and uncertainty, and it structures the whole evaluation.
whyNot: The cost of planning is normally small relative to the potential loss, and the loss is uncertain.
Planning is a cost rather than a benefit, and the later outcome is uncertain.
The distinction is about certainty, not cost classification.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a strong evaluative argument against detailed contingency planning?
options: You cannot plan for everything, so general resilience such as cash reserves may be better value
Disruptive events never happen to well-managed businesses
Contingency planning is prohibited by accounting standards
Insurance fully compensates for every possible loss
questions.why: General flexibility and financial strength protect against events nobody anticipated, which specific plans by definition cannot.
whyNot: Good management reduces some risks but cannot prevent external shocks.
Nothing in accounting standards prohibits it.
Insurance transfers financial loss and does not restore reputation or lost customers.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines scenario planning?
options: Preparing for several possible futures rather than forecasting a single one
Calculating the most likely sales figure for next year
Testing a product with a sample of customers
Recording what happened during a past crisis
questions.why: Scenario planning accepts that the future is uncertain and prepares for a range of outcomes.
whyNot: That is single-point forecasting.
That is market testing.
That is a post-incident review.

questions.stem: Why does the specification note that the planning process itself has value even if the event never occurs?
options: It exposes weaknesses in the business that are worth fixing anyway
It reduces the corporation tax the business pays
It removes the need for insurance
It guarantees the business will grow
questions.why: Working through how the business would cope reveals dependencies and gaps that can be addressed in normal trading.
whyNot: Planning has no direct tax effect.
Insurance often remains part of the response.
Resilience is not the same as growth.
